newsitem.title: GERMANY: German steel workers down tools to defend jobs.
newsitem.headline: German steel workers down tools to defend jobs.

text.p: Germany's major steelworks remained idle on Wednesday after unions vowed to fight the creation of a joint venture between steel giants Krupp and Thyssen which could cost 8,000 jobs.

Thousands of steel workers clad in white fire-proof overalls demonstrated at the Krupp Hoesch Stahl works in Dortmund against a job cuts plan presented to the works council at a meeting with company officials late on Tuesday.

Workers at the Thyssen Stahl plant in Duisburg also refused to go to work, continuing a week of stoppages since Fried. Krupp AG Hoesch-Krupp last week launched a hostile takeover bid for much larger rival steel group Thyssen AG.
Krupp dropped the bid after five days of talks with Thyssen in which the firms agreed to form a steel joint venture, hammering out the details over the next four weeks.
But this did not cool the tempers of workers fearing job losses in Germany's already depressed coal and steel heartland.

"If the companies need four weeks, then so do we," Juergen Hafner, chairman of the workers' council at the Krupp Hoesch Stahl plant, said late on Tuesday after being briefed by Krupp management and deciding to continue work stoppages.

Harald Schartau, head of the North Rhine-Westphalia arm of powerful steel and engineering union IG Metall, said the union would provide "massive resistance" to protest against the rationalisation moves.
After being informed on plans for the alliance, he said it would cost as many as 8,000 jobs over four to five years.
Many of the cuts would come at Krupp Hoesch Stahl, itself the product of a 1991 merger between Krupp and rival Hoesch AG, where blast furnace operations in Dortmund would be shut down.
Thyssen Stahl chairman Ekkehard Schulz was due to address steel workers at a gathering of employees later on Wednesday and outline the restructuring plans.
Hans-Wilhelm Grasshoff, the chief of Krupp's steel operation, told a workforce meeting late on Tuesday that Thyssen would take a 60 percent share in the venture.
The joint company will be founded on April 1, but production in the two companies' steel units is likely to continue as before until mid to late 1998, he said.
Thyssen AG chief executive Dieter Vogel said the consequences of a hostile takeover "would have been far worse than what will happen now that Thyssen will steer the fusion".
Speaking on German television he said Thyssen's steel operations, unlike Krupp's, were competitive even without the merger, but that the compromise was a "victory for reason".
"This is not about cutting jobs, but rather restructuring that will be accompanied by new technologies and considerable investments so that we remain competitive," Vogel said.
"Naturally, this cannot be done completely without reductions, but we will try to do this without lay-offs."
But so far the workers have not been convinced.

On Tuesday around 30,000 demonstrated in the financial capital Frankfurt outside the headquarters of Deutsche Bank to protest against the moral backing and huge financial support it and other banks had given to Krupp's original bid.

Unions, commentators and politicians saw the hostile bid as a shocking break with Germany's tradition of consensus between workers, banks, politicians and industry. Regional politicians put pressure on Krupp and Thyssen to sit down and negotiate.
Deutsche Bank chief executive Hilmar Kopper betrayed more than a hint of bitterness at the bank's annual news conference.

"The whole thing failed because of political intervention," he said. "It remains to be seen whether Thyssen and its employees will be better off under the solution that is now emerging than they would have been under a takeover."
-- Bonn Newsroom, 49 228 26097 150
